provenance.source_title: Towards Attuned AI: Integrating Care Ethics in Large Language Model Development and Alignment

research_problem.text: How can the ethics of care inform LLM development and value alignment, particularly where prevailing alignment approaches overlook individual circumstances, relationships, and vulnerability?

central_claims.text: Integrating care ethics into LLM design and value alignment offers a richer, more contextually grounded normative foundation than prevailing approaches.

evidence.text: We argue that integrating care ethics into the design and value alignment (VA) processes of LLMs offers a richer and more contextually grounded normative foundation for generative AI systems.

central_claims.text: LLMs often fail to respond appropriately to individual needs and social contexts because they apply overly generalized patterns of reasoning, making them ethically inadequate in emotionally sensitive domains.

evidence.text: These models often fail to respond appropriately to individual needs and social contexts because they apply overly generalized patterns of reasoning. This failure makes them ethically inadequate in emotionally sensitive domains.

The issue is not that these models operate on "simple" or "complicated" rules, but rather that their internal logic frequently fails to track the particularities that matter in real-world contexts, no matter how intricate it is.

central_claims.support_assessment: The claim attributes a frequent failure in emotionally sensitive uses specifically to overgeneralized reasoning and concludes that the models are ethically inadequate there. Section 2 offers the training-distribution argument and examples concerning mental-health chatbots, gender stereotypes, and benefit assessments. Those passages illustrate consequential insensitive or biased outputs, but the source does not establish how frequently they occur or show that overgeneralized reasoning, rather than another cause, produced each example. The examples support the concern without establishing the full frequency and causal scope of the claim.

central_claims.text: A static, well-defined training-data distribution cannot adequately represent the dynamic, messy real-world situations and users LLMs encounter.

evidence.text: The 'real world' where LLMs operate is rarely as neatly categorized as a static training distribution might suggest.
Human language and the world it reflects are inherently messy, with users and situations frequently existing in the 'margins' or as 'edge cases' that don't perfectly align with the training data.

central_claims.text: Because LLMs are scaled-up feed-forward neural networks trained using back-propagation, they are vulnerable to the same generalization problems attributed to those networks.

evidence.text: This limitation extends directly to modern Large Language Models (LLMs), which are, at their core, massively scaled-up versions of FFNNs trained using sophisticated forms of back-propagation [Rumelhart et al., 1985]. As such, they are vulnerable to the same generalization problems.

citations.reference_entry: David E Rumelhart, Geoffrey E Hinton, and Ronald J Williams. Learning Internal Representations by Error Propagation. 1985.

central_claims.support_assessment: This commits the authors to a transfer of the generalization limitation they discuss for feed-forward networks to modern LLMs. The preceding paragraphs invoke theoretical performance degradation away from training distributions and cite Marcus [1998] for neural-network failures on out-of-distribution data; this passage then asserts the architectural connection. Those reasons make the vulnerability plausible, but the source does not establish that architectural descent alone determines the extent or form of LLM failures. Its later examples concern LLM outputs, though they do not isolate that proposed mechanism.

central_claims.text: Therapy chatbots have exhibited discriminatory responses based on users’ conditions, perpetuating harmful stigmas.

evidence.text: In the realm of mental health, research has shown therapy chatbots exhibiting discriminatory responses based on users' conditions, perpetuating harmful stigmas [Harrison Dupre, 2025].

citations.reference_entry: Maggie Harrison Dupre. Stanford Research Finds That "Therapist" Chatbots Are Encouraging Users' Schizophrenic Delusions and Suicidal Thoughts. futurism.com, June 2025.

central_claims.text: LLMs have generated storytelling narratives that reinforce traditional gender stereotypes.

evidence.text: Regarding gender, LLMs have been found to generate narratives that reinforce traditional stereotypes in storytelling, demonstrating a clear gender bias in creative outputs [UCL, 2024].

citations.reference_entry: UCL. Large Language Models generate biased content, warn researchers. ucl.ac.uk, April 2024.

central_claims.text: Attempts to use AI to make benefit assessments fairer have reproduced existing human biases.

evidence.text: Furthermore, in the context of social services, attempts to implement AI for fairer benefit assessments have resulted in the reproduction of existing human biases, highlighting the challenge of achieving equitable outcomes through purely algorithmic means [Guo et al., 2024].

citations.reference_entry: Yufei Guo, Muzhe Guo, Juntao Su, Zhou Yang, Mengqiu Zhu, Hongfei Li, Mengyang Qiu, and Shuo Shuo Liu. Bias in Large Language Models: Origin, Evaluation, and Mitigation, November 2024.

central_claims.text: Bias in LLM outputs arises not only from training data but also from subjective values in human or AI feedback during alignment.

evidence.text: This bias is not solely a product of flawed training data but also arises from the subjective values embedded in human and even AI feedback during alignment processes.

central_claims.text: Dominant frameworks emphasizing abstract utility or generalized fairness are inadequate for addressing the nuanced biases the authors identify.

evidence.text: Consequently, relying on dominant moral frameworks that prioritize abstract utility or generalized fairness proves inadequate for addressing these nuanced biases.

Utilitarian approaches may justify sacrificing individual well-being for the sake of aggregated good, which is ethically troubling in contexts such as mental health or healthcare, where individual vulnerability and situational complexity demand more than mere utility maximization [Sola, 2023].

citations.reference_entry: Andrew Sola. Utilitarianism and Consequentialist Ethics: Framing the Greater Good. In Ethics and Pandemics: Interdisciplinary Perspectives on COVID-19 and Future Pandemics, pages 61-83. Springer Nature Switzerland, 2023.

central_claims.support_assessment: The inadequacy claim covers addressing the identified biases, not just identifying a possible ethical tension. The mental-health, gender, and benefit-assessment examples in §2 show the kinds of harms at issue; the normative-commitments discussion explains why aggregate-good reasoning can neglect an individual. The source does not compare outcomes under different frameworks or establish that utility- or fairness-oriented methods cannot address those biases when adapted. The offered reasons identify a limitation but do not establish inadequacy across the claim’s scope.

central_claims.text: Care ethics offers a crucial alternative for mitigating harms from misapplied generalization and fostering more equitable, sensitive AI systems.

evidence.text: The Ethics of Care, with its focus on attentiveness to individual needs and relational context, offers a crucial alternative for mitigating the harms of generalization and fostering more equitable and sensitive AI systems.
This shift could help mitigate the harmful consequences of misapplied generalizations and align AI systems more closely with the nuanced moral demands of human interaction.

central_claims.support_assessment: The proposed mitigation requires care-oriented training or design to change the harmful outputs described earlier in §2. The authors connect care ethics’ attention to needs and context to the failures illustrated by the three domain examples, but present neither an implemented method nor comparative results. The passages justify investigating the proposed alternative; they cannot determine whether it will mitigate the identified harms.

central_claims.text: LLM training and design should prioritize individual and contextual particularities rather than statistical generalization or broad generalizations that can misrepresent, exclude, or harm users.

evidence.text: Re-thinking the training and design of LLMs through the lens of EoC would entail prioritizing individual and contextual particularities rather than optimizing for statistical generalization.

Instead, we should aim for systems that are attuned to the particularities of individuals and their contexts of LLM usage, rather than imposing broad generalizations that may misrepresent, exclude, or even harm them.

central_claims.text: Care ethics’ compatibility with Ubuntu makes it a powerful decolonial alternative to dominant AI ethics frameworks.

evidence.text: Its compatibility with non-Western ethical traditions such as Ubuntu, "I am because we are", also makes it a powerful decolonial alternative to dominant AI ethics frameworks [Amugongo et al., 2023].

citations.reference_entry: Lameck Mbangula Amugongo, Nicola J. Bidwell, and Caitlin C. Corrigan. Invigorating Ubuntu Ethics in AI for healthcare: Enabling equitable care. In 2023 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency, pages 583-592, Chicago IL USA, June 2023. ACM.

central_claims.text: RLHF and RLAIF embody particular, non-neutral normative commitments, chiefly utilitarian and justice-based ones, through preference aggregation, fairness metrics, or constitutional principles.

evidence.text: Current Value Alignment (VA) methods, particularly Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and its more recent variant Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback (RLAIF), are grounded in specific normative frameworks, primarily utilitarianism and justice-based theories such as Contractualism and Rawlsian justice.

These approaches optimize behaviour either by aggregating human preferences (in RLHF), or by aligning model outputs with predefined fairness metrics or constitutional principles (in RLAIF), thus reflecting a commitment to maximizing overall utility or ensuring procedural fairness [Sola, 2023].

citations.reference_entry: Andrew Sola. Utilitarianism and Consequentialist Ethics: Framing the Greater Good. In Ethics and Pandemics: Interdisciplinary Perspectives on COVID-19 and Future Pandemics, pages 61-83. Springer Nature Switzerland, 2023.

central_claims.support_assessment: This classifies the normative commitments of RLHF and RLAIF generally, not merely one deployment. Section 2 describes their feedback or principle-based objectives, and later details Constitutional AI’s preference-model rewards. Those descriptions ground the authors’ interpretation, but the source does not analyze a range of implementations sufficient to establish the classification for both methods generally. Moving from optimization mechanics to a specifically utilitarian or justice-based ethical commitment also requires an interpretive premise, recorded under assumptions.

central_claims.text: Utilitarian approaches can justify sacrificing an individual’s well-being for aggregate good, which is troubling in vulnerable care contexts.

evidence.text: Utilitarian approaches may justify sacrificing individual well-being for the sake of aggregated good, which is ethically troubling in contexts such as mental health or healthcare, where individual vulnerability and situational complexity demand more than mere utility maximization [Sola, 2023].

citations.reference_entry: Andrew Sola. Utilitarianism and Consequentialist Ethics: Framing the Greater Good. In Ethics and Pandemics: Interdisciplinary Perspectives on COVID-19 and Future Pandemics, pages 61-83. Springer Nature Switzerland, 2023.

central_claims.text: Justice-based approaches can overemphasize truthfulness or impartiality and miss individuals’ emotional, relational, and contextual needs.

evidence.text: Likewise, justice-based approaches may overemphasize principles such as truthfulness or impartiality, and fail to account for the emotional, relational, and context-sensitive needs of individuals in morally complex or care-relevant situations [Gilligan, 1993].

citations.reference_entry: Carol Gilligan. In a Different Voice: Psychological Theory and Women's Development. Harvard University Press, 1993.

central_claims.text: Current reward- and rule-oriented value-alignment frameworks prove inadequate in care-relevant settings where needs are individual, emotionally laden, and context-dependent.

evidence.text: In such settings, the current VA frameworks, grounded in rule-following and aggregation, prove inadequate.

Examples include healthcare, education, eldercare, and mental health support, these fields in which the needs of individuals are unique, emotionally laden, and highly context-dependent [Beauchamp, 2006].

citations.reference_entry: Tom L. Beauchamp. The 'Four Principles' Approach to Health Care Ethics. In Principles of Health Care Ethics, pages 3-10. Wiley, 2006.

central_claims.support_assessment: The categorical 'prove inadequate' applies to current frameworks across the named settings. Section 2 explains potential conflicts between aggregate objectives or impartial rules and individual vulnerability; its mental-health example illustrates what the authors would want feedback to register instead. It does not test current frameworks in each named setting or show that they cannot accommodate relevant context. The reasons support a concern about limitations, but not the full categorical conclusion.

central_claims.text: Anthropic’s Constitutional AI states deontological commitments but ultimately selects responses by maximizing a preference-model reward; the authors conclude that its technical implementation could only be utilitarian.

evidence.text: In practice, while the constitution declares a duty-based moral stance, "do no harm," "be helpful," "be honest", the underlying alignment mechanism remains reward-driven: responses are ultimately chosen based on which maximizes the preference-model's score [Bai et al., 2022].

citations.reference_entry: Yuntao Bai et al. Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback, December 2022.

evidence.text: Thus, the case of Constitutional AI highlights the inadequacy of purely abstract approaches to the value alignment problem. As we have seen, although in principle, Anthropic adopted a deontological approach to value alignment, the technical implementation could only be utilitarian.

central_claims.support_assessment: The claim goes beyond describing a reward-maximization stage: 'could only be utilitarian' excludes another ethical interpretation or implementation of the technical process. Section 2 describes constitutional self-critique followed by an AI preference model supplying reinforcement-learning rewards, citing Bai et al. [2022]. That account supports the description of a reward-driven stage. It does not show that using a reward signal makes the overall method exclusively utilitarian, or that no other technical implementation is possible. The move from optimization mechanism to ethical identity depends on the interpretive premise recorded under assumptions.

central_claims.text: A value-alignment method inspired by care ethics and tailored to care-relevant domains and contexts is necessary.

evidence.text: Therefore, we argue that it is necessary to develop a value alignment method tailored to care-relevant domains and contexts inspired by the ethics of care.

Abstract, generalized principles, or the pursuit of aggregated preference maximization, often fail to adequately address the specific vulnerabilities, individual needs, and contextual particularities inherent in these domains.

central_claims.support_assessment: Necessity here concerns developing an alignment method for care-relevant contexts, not merely finding care ethics useful. Section 2 argues that abstract principles and aggregate preferences can miss vulnerabilities; its Constitutional AI discussion supplies one proposed illustration, and its chatbot example specifies the response features a care-informed method should attend to. These passages motivate the proposal. They do not establish that the approaches considered exhaust the ways to make alignment sensitive to vulnerability, or that such sensitivity requires a method inspired by care ethics. The necessity inference relies on the alternative-excluding premise recorded under assumptions.

central_claims.text: Developing AI systems genuinely aligned with human values, especially in contexts involving vulnerability, necessitates adopting ethical frameworks such as care ethics that are rooted in lived moral experience.

evidence.text: In this paper, we have argued that the development of AI systems genuinely aligned with human values, especially within contexts involving human vulnerabilities, necessitates the adoption of ethical frameworks such as care ethics, which are deeply rooted in the moral realities of lived experiences.
evidence.locator: §2, end of argument from normative commitments

central_claims.support_assessment: This necessity claim is broader than the preceding call for a care-inspired method in care-relevant domains: it concerns genuine alignment with human values, with particular emphasis on vulnerability. The generalization and normative-commitments arguments in §2 explain why the authors regard attention to lived circumstances as important. They do not establish that all routes to genuine alignment without an ethical framework of this kind are inadequate. The article’s stated conclusion therefore exceeds what its examples and conceptual comparisons establish.

central_claims.text: Existing RLHF and RLAIF methods can be modified to incorporate care-based principles, though the article does not provide a full technical method.

evidence.text: When it comes to the technical implementation of this VA method, current methods such as RLHF and RLAIF can be modified to incorporate care-based principles. However, the comprehensive elaboration of the full technical methodology is beyond the scope of this paper.

central_claims.text: A care-informed mental-health chatbot would weigh feedback against a user’s particular emotional state, relational cues, and expressed needs rather than reinforce responses simply because annotators rate them highly in general.

evidence.text: However, a care ethics-informed chatbot would go further by weighing feedback according to the user's current unique emotional state, relational cues, and expressed needs.
evidence.locator: §2, argument from normative commitments; chatbot example

evidence.text: Rather than reinforcing a response simply because it is rated highly in general by annotators, the model would be trained to identify morally salient features such as signs of vulnerability, dependency, or self-harm in this particular interaction and then be allowed to adjust its behaviour accordingly.
evidence.locator: §2, argument from normative commitments; chatbot example

central_claims.text: For a distressed user expressing suicidal thoughts, the proposed care-informed chatbot might prioritize empathy, safety, and relational responsibility over truthfulness.

evidence.text: A distressed user expressing suicidal thoughts might receive an AI response that prioritizes empathy, the user's safety, and relational responsibility over truthfulness.
evidence.locator: §2, argument from normative commitments; chatbot example

central_claims.support_assessment: The example makes an explicit tradeoff: truthfulness may be subordinated to empathy, safety, and relational responsibility for a user expressing suicidal thoughts. The preceding chatbot passages explain why the authors want feedback sensitive to this user’s emotional state instead of generic annotator preference. The article does not specify what an untruthful response would be, when it would improve safety, or how to adjudicate a conflict between safety and truthfulness. It therefore explains the intended priority without establishing that the tradeoff would be safe in practice.

central_claims.text: Care-based value alignment would train LLMs to attend to users’ emotional, social, and contextual needs rather than merely to rewards.

evidence.text: A care-based VA approach would train systems not merely to be reward-sensitive, but to be morally attentive, i.e. responsive to the emotional, social, and contextual needs of users.

central_claims.text: Care ethics would guide RLAIF to consider relational context and possible harms to vulnerable people and communities, rather than optimize solely for abstract utility or procedural fairness.

evidence.text: Rather than optimizing for abstract utility or procedural fairness, care ethics would guide alignment processes like RLAIF to consider the specific relational context and potential harms to vulnerable individuals and communities.

central_claims.text: Care ethics would encourage human labelers to consider the broader relational effects of AI responses, particularly for marginalized or care-dependent people, as well as individual preferences.

evidence.text: It would also inform the work of human labelers, encouraging them to reflect not only on individual preferences, but on the broader relational impacts of AI responses, especially for marginalized or care-dependent populations.

central_claims.text: In constitutional alignment, care ethics could supply a richer moral foundation by promoting the well-being of caregivers and care-receivers within interdependent social networks.

evidence.text: Constitutionally, care ethics could provide a richer moral foundation by promoting the well-being of both caregivers and care-receivers within interdependent social networks.

central_claims.text: Embedding a care-based moral orientation would make LLM chatbots more likely to resist sycophantic behavior.

evidence.text: By embedding this moral orientation, LLM's chatbots would be more likely to resist sycophantic behaviour, minimize hallucinations, and engage users with a deeper sense of responsibility and trust.

central_claims.support_assessment: The prediction concerns a lower likelihood of sycophancy after care ethics is embedded. Section 2 proposes context-weighted feedback and attention to vulnerability, but provides no mechanism connecting those changes specifically to resistance to sycophancy, and no evaluation of such a system. The source does not supply enough to assess the predicted effect.

central_claims.text: Embedding a care-based moral orientation would make LLM chatbots more likely to minimize hallucinations.

evidence.text: By embedding this moral orientation, LLM's chatbots would be more likely to resist sycophantic behaviour, minimize hallucinations, and engage users with a deeper sense of responsibility and trust.

central_claims.support_assessment: This predicts an improvement in hallucination behavior from embedding the proposed moral orientation. Section 2 discusses distributional generalization, bias, and context-weighted feedback, but does not explain why those changes would reduce hallucinations specifically or present tests of that outcome. The claimed link requires the unstated premise recorded under assumptions and is not established by the passages offered.

central_claims.text: Embedding a care-based moral orientation would make LLM chatbots more likely to engage users with a deeper sense of responsibility and trust.

evidence.text: By embedding this moral orientation, LLM's chatbots would be more likely to resist sycophantic behaviour, minimize hallucinations, and engage users with a deeper sense of responsibility and trust.

central_claims.text: Care ethics better reflects how people want to be treated in morally significant interactions with AI.

evidence.text: By offering a context-sensitive and relationally grounded framework, care ethics better reflects how people actually want to be treated in morally significant interactions with AI.

central_claims.support_assessment: This is a comparative generalization about people’s wishes in morally significant AI interactions. Section 1.2 presents care ethics’ account of particular needs and relationships, and §2 contrasts that account with aggregation and rule-based approaches. The source offers no study of users’ wishes and does not establish how broadly those wishes favor a care-based approach. The ethical comparison explains the authors’ rationale but cannot substantiate the empirical breadth of 'how people actually want to be treated.'

methodology.summary: A conceptual and normative argument in two parts: the authors connect LLM generalization failures to care ethics, then critique normative commitments attributed to existing value-alignment methods and propose care-informed alternatives. They use cited literature, reported examples, an account of Constitutional AI, and a hypothetical mental-health-chatbot scenario; they do not report developing or testing an alignment method.
methodology.study_design: Conceptual argument and literature-based critique, not an empirical evaluation of a care-informed model.
data_sources: Cited work on ethics of care, neural-network generalization, LLM bias, and alignment
Reported examples in mental health, storytelling, and benefit assessments
methodology.sample_or_scope: LLM development and value alignment, especially RLHF, RLAIF, and care-relevant settings including mental health, education, and social services.
analysis_methods: Normative comparison of care ethics with utilitarian and justice-based approaches
Conceptual argument concerning generalization and sensitivity to particular circumstances
Illustrative analysis of Constitutional AI and a proposed chatbot response

assumptions.text: For the claim that RLHF and RLAIF are chiefly utilitarian or justice-based, an optimization objective or feedback mechanism can be used to identify the ethical commitments of a value-alignment method.

For the claim that Constitutional AI’s implementation could only be utilitarian, maximizing preference-model scores makes the overall technical implementation utilitarian despite the role of constitutional constraints.
For the necessity of a care-inspired alignment method, ways of making alignment adequately responsive to vulnerability that do not draw on care ethics are insufficient.

For the proposed context-weighted chatbot training to work, relevant emotional, relational, and vulnerability cues can be identified reliably enough from an interaction to guide feedback and responses.
For the conclusion’s hallucination prediction, increasing a model’s care-oriented attention to users and context will also reduce the generation of unsupported or false content.

limitations.text: Care ethics’ contextual and relational character resists formalization and scalability; its lack of procedural structure can hinder transparency and consistency in automated systems.
A full technical methodology for modifying RLHF or RLAIF to incorporate care-based principles is beyond the article’s scope.
Recognizing complex emotional and social cues remains technically underdeveloped, and current models lack genuine understanding of vulnerability, dependency, and relational dynamics.
The article reports no implementation or evaluation of a care-informed alignment method, so its predicted behavioral benefits remain untested within the source.

proposed_solutions.text: Adapt LLM training, design, and value alignment to attend to individual needs, vulnerabilities, relationships, and circumstances rather than rely solely on abstract rules, aggregate preferences, or statistical generalization.
Modify RLHF or RLAIF feedback and reinforcement so models recognize morally salient features of particular interactions, such as emotional state, dependency, and risk of self-harm.
Use care ethics to inform human labeling and constitutional alignment, including attention to relational impacts and the well-being of caregivers and care-receivers.
Pursue further interdisciplinary research and cautious implementation when considering care ethics in AI design.

open_questions.text: How can care ethics’ contextual and relational principles be translated into a full technical value-alignment methodology while retaining transparency and consistency?
How reliably could an LLM identify vulnerability, dependency, emotional state, and relational cues and respond to them in a way that meaningfully constitutes care-based reasoning?
Would care-informed training actually reduce generalization harms, sycophancy, or hallucinations compared with existing alignment methods?
